title: EmeraldStack tenancy patterns and fallback sync
summary: Initial discovery focused on EmeraldStack's needs for reserved GPU capacity with tenant isolation, burst handling and predictable cost. Customer is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; leaning Dedicated with VPC/KMS requirements. Main concerns: warm pool prewarm times, noisy neighbor isolation, and fallback policies when reserved nodes are saturated.
next_steps: Redwood: send dedicated capacity pricing matrix and SLA options (by 2026-06-19)
Redwood SE: share benchmark template and perf run checklist
Customer: provide sample qps profile and peak window logs
Schedule technical deep dive with infra team week of 2026-06-22
action_items: Maya Chen - Send pricing matrix and high level contract terms by 2026-06-19
Liam O'Connor - Share benchmark template and suggested load pattern (within 2 business days)
Priya Malhotra - Export 7-day peak QPS telemetry and sample prompt distribution by 2026-06-20
transcript:
Meeting header: Date/Time: 2026-06-17 15:00 PDT; Duration: 49m; Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (EmeraldStack Head of Platform), Daniel (ML Infra), Sara (CTO)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro from Redwood side — I'm Maya, I'm the account lead, and Liam is our solutions engineer.
[00:18] Priya: Hi, I'm Priya. Thanks for setting this up. We wanted to talk through how you recommend we think about reserved GPUs and isolation — we run a multi-tenant API for embeddings and chat.
[00:32] Liam: Great. Can you give us a short profile of current traffic patterns? Avg qps, peak windows, tail latency expectations?
[00:45] Daniel: Sure. Avg inference qps is about 120 across the fleet, peaks hit ~1.8k for short bursts during nightly batch runs and sales spikes. 95th percentile latency SLO is 120ms for embeddings and 300ms for chat — those are what the app needs.
[01:12] Sara: We're trying to move away from a pure cloud GPU spot strategy because the preemption and noisy neighbor behavior gives unpredictable latency. We think Dedicated reserved capacity might be a better fit.
[01:29] Maya: Makes sense. A few things we usually ask: how strict is isolation — do you need physical tenancy, or are logical isolation and tenant fencing enough? Also any regulatory constraints for data residency or KMS?
[01:44] Priya: Logical isolation with strict network controls is okay for most workloads, but for a subset (PII/PHI experiments) we might need more strict separation. We need KMS integration and audit logs. SOC2 is required for vendor selection.
[02:05] Liam: Redwood Dedicated supports VPC-only modes and customer KMS via our Private deployment patterns; we can isolate workloads to dedicated GPU pools and also offer stronger tenancy where required. The tradeoff is cost vs utilization.
[02:24] Daniel: On burst modeling — how do you recommend handling 1.8k qps spikes that last 5-15 minutes? Do we prewarm a hot pool, rely on burst capacity, or have fallbacks to smaller quantized models?
[02:38] Liam: Usually a mix. We recommend a prewarmed hot pool sized to absorb the first wave (based on tail latency), with automatic fallback routing to quantized variants or hosted endpoints when the dedicated pool is saturated. Also prefix/KV cache helps for chat reuse.
[02:56] Priya: What's the warm start time? If we add nodes, how long until they're usable for inference?
[03:05] Liam: Cold start differs by instance type and model — for a 70B model on our infra, typical prewarm to usable state is ~3-6 minutes if pre-loading weights, but with efficient snapshotting and container reuse you can get sub-2 minute times for smaller models. We also recommend keeping a minimal warm buffer to avoid that ramp.
[03:28] Speaker 2 (Sara?): Ok, so we probably need a buffer equivalent to ~200 qps of capacity always warm.
[03:36] Maya: That's a good initial heuristic. For cost optimization we can propose autoscaling thresholds and burst credit that allows short spikes without reserving full capacity.
[03:48] Daniel: Does Redwood offer per-tenant throttling or hard caps at the platform level?
[03:55] Liam: Yes, we have per-tenant quotas and rate limiting with token-level tracking; plus tenant fencing at the scheduler layer to avoid noisy neighbor issues.
[04:12] Priya: Security question — how does key management work? We need customer-managed keys and separation so Redwood does not have decryption capability.
[04:21] Liam: We can integrate with your KMS (AWS KMS/GCP KMS/HashiCorp) and in Private mode, keys remain under your control. For Hosted Dedicated we offer envelope encryption with customer keys stored in KMS; access controls and logs are surfaced in the Redwood Console.
[04:40] Sara: What about auditability? We need token-level audit logs for regulatory review.
[04:46] Maya: Our Console exposes token-level usage, per-request metadata, and you can export logs to your SIEM. For Private on-prem we can set up direct log forwarding as well.
[05:00] Daniel: Okay. Let's talk about failover: if our dedicated pool saturates, and you route to a hosted fallback, how do you preserve data residency and security constraints?
[05:12] Liam: We can set policy-based routing: if model or tenant requires VPC-only, then the fallback is to a compatible model in the same control plane or to a private reserve. If you require strict on-prem processing, then we can only allow fallbacks that meet the same tenancy. We'll include the policy language in the SLA.
[05:34] Priya: We will need clear RTO/RPO for those fallbacks and probably an ops playbook for when the warm pool depletes.
[05:42] Maya: We'll draft a playbook: warm pool thresholds, alarming, auto-scale actions, and manual escalation steps.
[05:50] [07:10] Priya: Another area — how do you measure and bill for burst capacity? Is it time-based or token-based? We don't want surprise costs for 15-minute spikes.
[07:23] Maya: There are a few pricing models: reserved monthly capacity + metered burst (per vGPU-minute) or a committed burst tier that gives you a pool of burst credits. We'll include examples in the pricing matrix so you can model cost for your observed traffic profile.
[07:41] Daniel: Do you support model quantization to reduce cost? We have research teams that can accept slightly lower quality for certain batches.
[07:50] Liam: Yes. We can provide quantized variants (8-bit/4-bit where viable) and recommend model variants per workload. We've got tooling in Redwood Optimize to estimate quality vs latency tradeoffs.
[08:05] Sara: Are there any hard limits on concurrency per GPU we should know?
[08:12] Liam: Concurrency depends on model size, sequence length, and kernels. For example, a 13B model might support hundreds of concurrent short requests per A100; a 70B will support far fewer. We'll run a benchmark with your prompts to size correctly.
[08:29] Maya: Can you share a sample of the prompt mix and average token lengths? That will feed into our sizing.
[08:36] Priya: We'll extract that today and share the token histogram and peak time windows.
[08:44] [10:02] Daniel: For SLA, we need 99.9% uptime for Dedicated during business hours and 99.5% overall. Is that something you offer?
[10:12] Maya: We offer tiered SLAs. 99.9% for dedicated pools is an option on an Enterprise contract with reserved capacity and on-call support. We should add details into the contract template.
[10:24] Priya: What about maintenance windows and preemptions — how often can we expect planned downtime?
[10:30] Liam: Planned maintenance is typically scheduled with at least 48-hour notice; we offer maintenance windows and can coordinate for low-traffic periods. For Dedicated Reserved we avoid forceful eviction for maintenance except in extreme cases.
[10:45] Sara: Can you support a hybrid model where some tenants land on Dedicated and others on Hosted, but with the same API surface?
[10:55] Maya: Yes — that's a core Redwood design. We can route by tenant, model, or route; the API and SDK are consistent. That simplifies fallbacks and rollouts.
[11:08] Priya: On the security checklist — do you have SOC2 certs and can you share pen test reports?
[11:15] Maya: Yes, we have SOC2 Type II and we'll send the security whitepaper and SOC2 attestation. For pen tests we can share a redacted summary; for deeper reports we'll talk through an NDA.
[11:28] Daniel: Ok good. Next, latency: you mentioned KV/prefix caching — our chat workload has high reuse across sessions. How effective is that for cost reduction?
[11:40] Liam: Very effective. If prompts share long prefixes or similar system prompts, prefix caching reduces token re-computation and can shave 30–60% of per-request compute in some chat patterns. We'll analyze your prompt histograms to estimate savings.
[11:58] [14:00] Priya: We're also worried about noisy neighbors within a dedicated pool — if a tenant does a large batch, can they starve others?
[14:12] Liam: That's why we have tenant fencing—scheduler-level reservations and throttles. Also we recommend isolating heavy batch jobs to a separate pool or using burst credits so they don't impact real-time serving.
[14:26] Sara: For dedicated pools, do you expose VM-level telemetry or is it aggregated? We need fine-grained logs for incident investigations.
[14:36] Maya: We provide per-instance and per-request metrics on the Console and can export to your monitoring stack (Prometheus/Grafana, Datadog). For Private deployments we can forward raw telemetry directly.
[14:50] Daniel: Can we run a 2-hour perf test simulating our peak with your SEs to validate the warm pool sizing?
[14:58] Liam: Absolutely. We'll propose a benchmark plan — step up to peak qps, measure p95/p99 latency, and test fallback behavior. We'll need the prompt set and token distribution.
[15:10] Priya: Timeline wise — we want to be production-ready with reserved capacity in Q3. Ideally pilot in July.
[15:18] Maya: That fits. Steps would be: share telemetry, Redwood runs benchmark, produce sizing + pricing, sign pilot commitment, run pilot and validate.
[15:28] [20:00] Daniel: Are there any gotchas we should watch for when migrating model versions? We sometimes roll fast.
[20:10] Liam: Model versioning and canary rollouts are supported. For Dedicated we recommend canarying on a small warm subset first and tracing quality regressions. We can snapshot KV caches to reduce cold starts during rollouts.
[20:25] Priya: If we need more strict tenancy for the PII experiments, what is the delta on cost? Rough estimate?
[20:32] Maya: Physical dedicated tenancy increases unit cost — depends on instance type and utilization but expect a 20–40% premium over logical isolation, due to lower consolidation. We'll include scenarios in the pricing doc.
[20:45] Sara: For encryption at rest, we need HSM-backed keys for certain datasets. Is that supported?
[20:52] Liam: We can integrate with customer HSM via KMS providers or you can run Redwood Private on-prem where keys never leave your environment. We'll capture that requirement.
[21:05] [28:00] Priya: A practical question — how long does procurement usually take for Dedicated customers? We need to align internal timelines.
[28:08] Maya: It varies, but for Enterprise deals with Reserved capacity and standard security reviews, 4–8 weeks is typical once the SOW is agreed. Procurement lead times may add a couple weeks depending on legal.
[28:20] Daniel: Do you have reference customers with similar patterns we can talk to?
[28:25] Maya: Yes, we can share anonymized references; I'll include two customers with similar multi-tenant embeddings workloads.
[28:34] Priya: Great. Can we also get an example SLO/SLA doc and incident response commitments?
[28:40] Maya: Yes — we'll send that along with the pricing matrix.
[28:46] [36:00] Liam: For the benchmark plan, we propose a 2-hour simulated peak, a 1-hour steady state at target average qps, and an attack window to validate fallback. We'll provide the script and instrumentation steps.
[36:15] Daniel: That sounds fine. We'll need to block time with our infra team for the run.
[36:22] Priya: One more thing — are there guardrails in the Console to prevent accidental capacity spikes from a tenant misconfiguration?
[36:30] Liam: Yes, there are quota controls, plus automated anomaly detection that can trigger throttles and alerts. You can also set soft and hard caps per tenant.
[36:40] Sara: For billing, will usage be visible in near real time?
[36:44] Maya: Yes, our console shows token-level usage and a cost breakout per tenant; you can set budget alerts.
[36:52] [42:00] Priya: Ok, let's recap next steps. We'll share telemetry and prompt histograms. Redwood will send pricing, SLA, security docs, and benchmark plan. Then schedule a technical deep dive/benchmark run.
[42:15] Maya: Correct. Action items we'll enumerate in email. Any final questions?
[42:22] Daniel: Not from me.
[42:24] Sara: All good.
[42:26] Priya: Thanks everyone.
[42:30] Maya: Thanks for your time — we'll follow up with the materials earlier this week.
[42:36] [49:00] End recording
